awd_titl_txt: REDWOODS: A hybrid wavefront sensor / science camera to demonstrate extreme exoplanet imaging at Lick observatory
awd_abstract_narration:
Over 5000 exoplanets have been discovered to date, but only a handful of these exoplanets have been directly imaged. Direct imaging requires detecting the exoplanet’s light despite the glare of its host star, but the exoplanet is millions to billions of times fainter than than its host star. Exoplanets that have been directly imaged so far are large and bright like Jupiter. Detecting Earth-like exoplanets that could have life on their surface is the next goal, but this requires instruments that are at least 100 times more sensitive. The investigators will test new technologies designed to bridge this gap. This testing will take place on the Shane Telescope at Lick Observatory in California. In addition, the team will engage undergraduate summer students from underrepresented groups to work on this project, and they will develop educational programs with local high schools. 

The main factor currently limiting exoplanet imaging instrument sensitivity is residual “speckle” noise, which limits exoplanetary signal detection in science images. Speckles originate from a combination of (1) errors left over after an adaptive optics (AO) system has made an initial correction of the atmospheric turbulence, and (2) imperfections in the optical surfaces from the telescope and instrument. This program will implement a new pathfinder wavefront sensing technology at Lick Observatory on the Shane telescope’s AO system (ShaneAO) called the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera Technique (FAST), designed to overcome this speckle noise limit. This project to implement FAST at ShaneAO is called Real-time Exoplanet Direct imager via Wavefront control Of Optical DefectS (REDWOODS). REDWOODS is a focal plane wavefront sensor (WFS) and coronagraphic imager that will demonstrate the technology needed to enable new exoplanet imaging science on future 30m-class telescopes. REDWOODS will also enable a simultaneous Z-H band Pyramid WFS, demonstrating new capabilities of this WFS technology. This project will engage undergraduate summer students to work on REDWOODS, which will contribute to the Cal-Bridge Program, a program to increase PhDs amongst underrepresented groups within California’s public university systems. The team will also develop the Santa Cruz Extreme AO Laboratory portable unit project (SEALpup)—a hands-on portable REDWOODS demo for education and public outreach.

por.por_cntn:
Are we alone in the Universe? This project aims to help answer this fundamental question to humanity by developing technologies to enable imaging planets around starts beyond the Solar System–called exoplanets–that harbor life on their surface. Large 30m-wide telescopes are currently being built to enable this high-priority habitable exoplnaet imaging science goal, but current state-of-the-art technologies must also improve instrument detection sensitivity by 100x for this goal to be posible. This project developed three technologies to help bridge this 100x gap: (1) a new type of sensor–called the fast atmospheric self-coherent camera technique, or FAST–that enables a combination of coronagraphic (i.e., blocking out starlight but not exoplanet light) imaging and enhanced high-speed correction of residual leftover scattered starlight, (2) a new type of sensor–called an unmodulated fully reflective 3 sided pyramid wavefront sensor (3RPWFS)--that  improves the compensation of starlight propagating through Earth’s atmospheric turbulence with a technique called adaptive optics (AO), and (3) a new type of AO software–called multi-wavefront sensor single conjugate AO control (multi-WFS SCAO)–that enables sensors 1 and 2 to work more efficiently within existing AO systems. The project developed an instrument, called REDWOODS, within the ShaneAO system on the 3m-wide Shane telescope at Lick Observatory to test these three capabilities on starlight for the first time. The FAST and 3RPWFS instrument hardware was first designed, then fabricated at the component level, then assembled and aligned, and then installed within the ShaneAO system. The multi-WFS SCAO software was developed and validated on the installed REDWOODS instrument internally, after which the Shane telescope directed starlight into the REDWOODS instrument. All three technologies were validated on starlight. The so called “on-sky” validation of these three technologies for the first time sets the stage for their implementation within instrumentation at larger telescopes to help enable habitable exoplanet imaging. This project also supported the training and professional development of undergraduate and graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. The project also developed a hands-on technology demonstration kit for public outreach, which was implemented at the STEM San Joaquin event in fall 2025.
